title: 1 Kings 12:25–33
context: Jeroboam fortifies Shechem and Penuel, but, fearing that worship in Jerusalem will draw the people back to Rehoboam, he sets up golden calves at Bethel and Dan, echoing Aaron’s calf, appoints non-Levitical priests, and creates a feast in the eighth month ‘devised of his own heart.’ The narrator calls this a sin, and Kings later remembers it as the sin of Jeroboam. Both traditions read the passage as shared ground about fear displacing faith and the dangers of self-made worship.

verses.text: Then Jeroboam built Shechem in the hill country of Ephraim, and lived in it; and he went out from there and built Penuel.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jeroboam builds Shechem in the hill country of Ephraim and lives there, then builds Penuel. He secures his realm.

Arminian readers see a new king establishing his capital and defenses.
verses.reformedNotes:
Shechem and Penuel both have patriarchal associations (compare Genesis 12:6; 32:30–31). Their precise role in Jeroboam’s strategy is not spelled out.

Reformed readers see a king consolidating power. Both traditions read this plainly as shared ground and hold geographic details lightly.

verses.text: Jeroboam said in his heart, “Now the kingdom will return to David’s house.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jeroboam reasons in his heart that the kingdom might return to David’s house. Fear begins to shape his decisions.

Arminian readers see fear overriding trust in God’s promise of 11:38.
verses.reformedNotes:
God had promised to be with Jeroboam if he obeyed. Jeroboam relies instead on his own calculation.

Reformed readers see unbelief at the root of his coming sin. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the danger of fear displacing faith.

verses.text: If this people goes up to offer sacrifices in the LORD’s house at Jerusalem, then the heart of this people will turn again to their lord, even to Rehoboam king of Judah; and they will kill me, and return to Rehoboam king of Judah.”
verses.arminianNotes:
He fears that worship in Jerusalem will turn the people’s hearts back to Rehoboam, and they will kill him. Political anxiety drives him.

Arminian readers see Jeroboam choosing self-protection over obedience.
verses.reformedNotes:
Jeroboam sees the temple as a threat to his throne. His reasoning is entirely political.

Reformed readers see worship being subordinated to power. Both traditions read this as shared ground, noting that his fear contradicts the conditional promise God had given him.

verses.text: So the king took counsel, and made two calves of gold; and he said to them, “It is too much for you to go up to Jerusalem. Look and behold your gods, Israel, which brought you up out of the land of Egypt!”
verses.arminianNotes:
Jeroboam makes two golden calves and tells Israel, “Behold your gods, Israel, which brought you up out of the land of Egypt!” His words echo Exodus 32:4.

Arminian readers see a deliberate choice that repeats Israel’s earliest idolatry.
verses.reformedNotes:
The echo of Aaron’s calf is unmistakable. Jeroboam presents the calves as a convenience.

Reformed readers see false worship dressed as practical reform. Both traditions read this as clear shared ground about idolatry, whatever the calves were meant to represent.

verses.text: He set the one in Bethel, and the other he put in Dan.
verses.arminianNotes:
He sets one calf in Bethel and the other in Dan. The shrines frame his kingdom.

Arminian readers see worship organized around political boundaries rather than God’s command. Convenience becomes the measure of worship.
verses.reformedNotes:
Bethel had associations with Jacob (Genesis 28:19), and Dan with earlier irregular worship (Judges 18:30).

Reformed readers see a counterfeit system rooted in old places. Both traditions read this plainly as shared ground, holding the exact locations and purposes of the shrines with appropriate caution.

verses.text: This thing became a sin, for the people went even as far as Dan to worship before the one there.
verses.arminianNotes:
This becomes a sin, for the people go as far as Dan to worship. The narrator gives his verdict.

Arminian readers see a king leading his people into sin by his choices.
verses.reformedNotes:
The people follow Jeroboam’s lead. The ‘sin of Jeroboam’ becomes a refrain in Kings (compare 2 Kings 17:21–22).

Reformed readers see leaders bearing heavy responsibility for the worship of those they lead. Both traditions read this as shared ground about idolatry’s spreading effect.

verses.text: He made houses of high places, and made priests from among all the people, who were not of the sons of Levi.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jeroboam builds shrines on high places and appoints priests from all the people, not from the Levites. He replaces God’s order.

Arminian readers see a deliberate departure from the law’s pattern for worship.
verses.reformedNotes:
Priesthood was reserved for Aaron’s line and the Levites in the law. Jeroboam sets that aside.

Reformed readers see worship reshaped by human design. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the importance of worshiping God as he directs, without inventing a dispute about salvation.

verses.text: Jeroboam ordained a feast in the eighth month, on the fifteenth day of the month, like the feast that is in Judah, and he went up to the altar. He did so in Bethel, sacrificing to the calves that he had made, and he placed in Bethel the priests of the high places that he had made.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jeroboam ordains a feast in the eighth month, like Judah’s feast, and sacrifices to the calves at Bethel, installing the priests he made. He imitates while altering.

Arminian readers see a counterfeit calendar replacing the one God gave.
verses.reformedNotes:
The feast resembles the Feast of Booths, held in the seventh month (Leviticus 23:34). Jeroboam shifts it.

Reformed readers see self-made worship. Both traditions read this as shared ground, noting the narrator’s emphasis on what Jeroboam ‘had made.’

verses.text: He went up to the altar which he had made in Bethel on the fifteenth day in the eighth month, even in the month which he had devised of his own heart; and he ordained a feast for the children of Israel, and went up to the altar to burn incense.
verses.arminianNotes:
He goes up to the altar at Bethel on the fifteenth day of the eighth month, ‘the month which he had devised of his own heart,’ to burn incense. His worship is his own invention.

Arminian readers see personal invention replacing obedience.
verses.reformedNotes:
The narrator’s phrase ‘devised of his own heart’ sums up the problem.

Reformed readers see worship that serves human ends rather than God’s glory. Both traditions read this as clear shared ground, and 1 Kings 13 follows with a prophet’s word against this altar.
